chapters.t: Why they kept getting it wrong

caps.t:
At Bikini Atoll in July 1946, the US
Navy set off an atomic bomb under its own
fleet.

It threw up a column of water
about 2,000 feet across,

and it climbed more than a mile before
it all came back down on the ships.

Afterwards, the sailors
couldn't wash those ships clean,

and inside three weeks, the Army's radiation
safety doctor was demanding a halt.

And that was only the first of three times
America lost its grip on its own bomb.
Eight years later, at the same atoll,

a hydrogen bomb came out two and a half
to three times bigger than planned.

Its radioactive ash came down on
islanders and on a Japanese fishing boat.

Then in 1962, a bomb set off
250 miles above the Pacific,
lit up the night sky over Hawaii,
and crippled satellites in orbit.

And you have to ask why the
experts kept missing it.

The war had been over for less than a year
when the Navy decided it needed to know

what an atomic bomb would
do to a fleet of warships.

So, it gathered more than 90 old and
captured ships in the lagoon at Bikini,
out in the Marshall Islands.
It even put live animals on some of them,

mostly pigs, goats, and rats, to see what
the blast and the radiation would do.

But first, the people who
lived on Bikini had to go.

In early March 1946, about 160
of them were taken to Rongerik,
a much smaller atoll about 125 miles away.

The Navy filmed the
meeting where their leader,

Juda, agreed to it, although the scene
you see was restaged for the cameras.

In it, he says they're willing to go
and that everything is in God's hands.
Then on July 1st came the first test,
called Able.
A B-29 dropped the bomb over the fleet,

and according to the Joint
Chiefs Evaluation Board,

it missed the target ship
by 1,500 to 2,000 feet.

Five ships went down, though most
of the fleet was still afloat.
But there was a problem.
The next test was about to show,

and it had nothing to
do with sinking ships.

On July 25th, the Navy hung the
second bomb 90 feet under the water,

below a landing ship right
in the middle of the fleet.

It was about the same size as
the one dropped on Nagasaki.

When it went off, it threw up a column of
water about 2,000 feet across and 6,000

feet tall, something like
a million tons of it.

Then it fell back, and a ring of radioactive
mist rolled out across the lagoon and
over the ships.
The aircraft carrier Saratoga,
one of the closest big ships to the blast,
sank seven and a half hours later.
And the Japanese battleship Nagato,

which had come through Able,
went down a few days after that.

But it got worse for the
ships that were still afloat.

That mist had left
radioactive material on them,
far more than anyone had predicted.

The Joint Chiefs board said those
ships had become radioactive stoves,

which would have burned
all living things aboard.

And Life magazine later worked out
that if they'd been fully crewed,

the Baker bomb would
have killed 35,000 men.

So the Navy sent sailors
back aboard to clean them.

They scrubbed the decks,
they sprayed them,
and they painted them, but it didn't work.

Unless they sandblasted a
ship down to bare metal,
the radiation just stayed where it was.

The Army doctor in charge of radiation
safety was Colonel Stafford Warren.

On August 7th, he wrote a secret memo
saying the target ships were extensively

contaminated with dangerous
amounts of radioactivity.

It was hiding in crevices
where the hoses couldn't reach,

and some ships, he wrote, had
many lethal doses on them.
Worse, some of it was plutonium,

which he warned was hard to detect and
insidiously toxic in very small amounts.
The admiral running the tests,
William Blandy, wasn't convinced at first,

but that didn't last because
Warren showed him a fish.

He'd laid a fish from the lagoon
on a sheet of photographic film,

and the radiation inside it had printed
a picture of the fish all by itself.

Warren wrote home afterwards that
the fish's self x-ray did the trick,

and on August 10th, Blandy
stopped the cleanup.

Three days later, Warren
was writing again,

calling the alpha emitters on the ships
the most poisonous chemical known.

The planned third test, deep
on the bottom of the lagoon,
was cancelled.
By then, the Navy had no clean ships left,

and officials just said they
didn't need the test anymore.
Eight years later, back at the same atoll,
the scientists got the bomb itself wrong.

By 1954, America was
testing hydrogen bombs,

many times stronger
than the bombs of 1946.

The one called Castle Bravo
was set for March 1st,
again at Bikini.

Its designers expected
about five or six megatons,

which is roughly the force of
five or six million tons of TNT.
Its fuel was made with lithium,

and they believed most of that lithium
would just sit there and do nothing.

But in the heat of the
blast, it joined in,
and it added a huge amount of extra power.
Bravo came out at 15 megatons,
which is about a thousand Hiroshimas,

and it's still the biggest the
United States has ever set off.

Within seconds, the fireball was
more than three miles across,
and the cloud climbed past 100,000 feet.

It left a crater in the reef about
6,500 feet wide and 250 feet deep.

Its fallout spread over something like
7,000 square miles of ocean and islands.

So, the bomb was a surprise, and
the cloud turned out to be one too.

Going by the forecast, the planners had
judged that no fallout would reach the
inhabited islands, so the shot went ahead.

For years afterwards, officials blamed
it on an unexpected shift in the wind.

But a 2013 study for the Defense
Department called that story a legend.

It said the fallout came from the huge cloud
a blast on the coral surface had thrown
into the stratosphere.
Even at the planned size, it said,

the inhabited atolls would
still have been contaminated.

And Los Alamos had warned about 10 days
before the test that the yield could go as
high as it did.

A few hours after the blast, a fine
white ash began falling on Rongelap,
more than a hundred miles to the east.

82 people were on Rongelap
and nearby Ailinginae.

Their children played in the
white powder as if it were snow,
and some of them even ate it.

28 American servicemen at a weather
station on Rongerik got caught in it too.

But it was two days before the
people of Rongelap were taken off,

and by then, the fallout
had already landed on them.

In all, 236 islanders
were moved off Rongelap,
Ailinginae, and Utirik.
And about 80 miles east of Bikini,

just outside the danger zone
the Americans had marked,

a Japanese tuna boat called the Lucky
Dragon Number Five was out fishing.

Its 23 crewmen saw a bright
light change the sky,

and then they heard a deep rumble that
seemed to come from under the sea.
One of them, Matashichi Oishi,

said later that the white ash hit them in
the face and covered the deck so thickly
that it held their footprints,
and he said he licked it.

By the time they got home
to Japan two weeks later,
the crew were sick with radiation.

That September, their
chief radio operator,

Aikichi Kuboyama, became
the first of them to die.

People in Japan, and
then around the world,

began demanding an end to
nuclear tests in the open air.
India's Prime Minister, Jawaharlal Nehru,
said that no country, however powerful,
was safe from destruction.
But America kept testing, and by 1962,

it wanted to know what a nuclear blast
would do far above the atmosphere.

The first try, that June, failed when the
rocket's engine cut out about a minute

after launch, so the missile had to
be destroyed over Johnston Island.
On the night of July 8th, Hawaii time,
they tried again.

A Thor rocket carried a 1.4
megaton bomb about 250 miles up,

and it went off over the Pacific
just after 11:00 at night.
In Hawaii, more than 700 miles away,
the night sky lit up in red and green,
like a man-made aurora.

One atomic veteran said later that some
hotels even held rooftop parties to watch.

On Oahu, streetlights went out
and burglar alarms went off,

although later studies say far fewer
lights failed than the stories claim.
But the real damage was higher up,

in the belts of radiation
that circle the Earth.
The blast poured electrons into them,

and it made the inner belt at least a
hundred times more intense than nature had.

And the next day,
America launched Telstar,

the first satellite to send
live TV across the Atlantic,

and it flew right through
all that new radiation.

NASA says it took a dose a hundred
times bigger than expected.

Telstar's electronics started
failing that November,

and by February 1963, it
had gone silent for good.

It's still up there, though
it's been dead for decades.

NASA counts seven satellites
lost within months of the test,
most of them from damaged solar cells.

And NASA's David Sibeck says how bad the
new radiation belt was and how long it
lasted came as a surprise.

Looking back at all three, we'd say
the bombs weren't really the problem.

Each time, the people running the tests
trusted their forecasts and estimates more

than the evidence allowed
and went ahead anyway.

Los Alamos had even warned that
Bravo could reach 15 megatons.

Still, the islanders of Rongelap were left
in its path because the planners' rule
was to avoid moving them if they could,

and most of the people who
paid for it were never asked.

The families of Bikini never
got to move back home for good,

and the Lucky Dragon's crew
had only been out fishing.
Then on August 5th, 1963, America,

the Soviet Union, and Britain signed a
treaty in Moscow banning nuclear tests in the

atmosphere, in outer
space, and underwater.

Every one of the three tests in this
story had happened in one of those places.
The US Senate approved it that September,
and it came into force on October 10th.
It left underground tests alone,
though, and those went on for decades.

Our next story is a bomb America
never meant to set off at all,

dropped off the coast of
Georgia in 1958 and never found.
